title: Azure Data Engineer (DP-203)
disclaimer: Independent practice material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Microsoft. Confers no certificate. All scenarios are original; no exam content is reproduced.

scenarios.title: The rename failure
scenarios.situation: A data lake on regular Blob storage can't atomically rename directories, breaking Spark job commits.
choices: Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 — hierarchical namespace enables atomic directory operations for analytics engines
scenarios.why: ADLS Gen2's hierarchical namespace brings true directories with atomic renames — which Spark and Hadoop rely on for commit protocols. Flat blob namespaces emulate folders and can't guarantee atomic directory operations.
scenarios.hint: Which storage flavor gives you real directories with atomic renames?

scenarios.title: The CSV swamp
scenarios.situation: A lake stores everything as CSV. Queries scan full files, schemas drift, and there's no way to update a single record.
scenarios.prompt: What file format should the curated zone use?
choices: Parquet (columnar) — or Delta Lake on Parquet for ACID, time travel, and upserts
scenarios.why: Parquet's columnar layout means queries read only needed columns (massive scan reduction); Delta Lake adds ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel on top. CSV is the raw-landing format, not the curated-zone format.
scenarios.hint: Columnar reads plus transactions — which format family?

scenarios.title: The full-scan query
scenarios.situation: Analysts query a 50 TB sales table filtered by month, but every query scans all 50 TB.
choices: Partitioning by date (e.g., year=/month= folders) — partition pruning skips irrelevant data
scenarios.why: Partitioning organizes data so the engine prunes (skips) partitions outside the filter — a month query reads 1/60th of 5 years. Without partitioning, every query pays the full-scan price.
scenarios.hint: How do you make a month-filtered query skip the other 59 months?

scenarios.title: The medallion
scenarios.situation: Raw feeds land in all shapes; analysts need clean, conformed tables; data scientists want feature-ready aggregates.
scenarios.why: Medallion (bronze/silver/gold) structures the lake by refinement: immutable raw landing, validated conformed data, then business aggregates. Each layer has clear quality contracts and consumers.
scenarios.hint: Raw, cleaned, business-ready — what are the three layers called?

scenarios.title: The hot raw data
scenarios.situation: Raw landing data stays on Hot tier forever though nobody reads landings older than 90 days.
choices: Lifecycle management policies — e.g., Hot→Cool at 90 days, →Archive at 365
scenarios.why: Lifecycle policies automate tier transitions by age/last-access — the cost control for append-only lake landings. Archive tier suits compliance retention; Cool suits occasional reprocessing.
scenarios.hint: How do you age data down the tiers automatically?

scenarios.title: The million tiny files
scenarios.situation: Streaming ingestion writes one small JSON file per event — 2 million files a day. Spark jobs now take hours just listing files.
scenarios.prompt: What is the problem and fix?
choices: Small-file problem — compact/merge files (auto-compaction, streaming checkpoints with larger triggers) to right-size files
scenarios.why: Analytics engines pay per-file overhead (listing, opening, metadata); millions of tiny files destroy performance. Compaction merges them into optimally-sized files (hundreds of MB); streaming sinks should batch appropriately.
scenarios.hint: Millions of tiny files kill Spark. What file hygiene fixes it?

scenarios.title: The hardcoded server
scenarios.situation: Fifty pipelines hardcode the SQL server name. A migration to a new server means editing all fifty.
scenarios.prompt: What ADF design centralizes connection info?
choices: Linked services — define the connection once; datasets and pipelines reference it
scenarios.why: Linked services encapsulate connection information (server, auth via managed identity/Key Vault) as reusable named resources. Change the server once in the linked service — all fifty pipelines follow.
scenarios.hint: Where should connection details live so fifty pipelines share one definition?

scenarios.title: The on-prem source
scenarios.situation: A pipeline must copy data from an on-premises SQL Server behind the corporate firewall — no inbound ports allowed.
choices: Self-hosted IR — installed on-premises, makes outbound-only connections to ADF
Azure IR — can't reach behind the firewall
SSIS IR — for SSIS packages, not this
scenarios.why: The self-hosted integration runtime runs inside your network and initiates outbound connections to Data Factory — no inbound firewall rules. Azure IR handles cloud sources; SSIS IR lifts SSIS packages.
scenarios.hint: Which IR reaches on-premises data without inbound firewall rules?

scenarios.title: The legacy packages
scenarios.situation: The company has 300 SSIS packages with complex logic that must run in Azure with minimal rewrite.
choices: Azure-SSIS integration runtime — lift-and-shift SSIS execution in ADF
Rewriting all 300 as ADF pipelines immediately
scenarios.why: The SSIS IR provisions the SSIS engine in ADF so existing packages run with minimal change — the pragmatic bridge while teams modernize package by package.
scenarios.hint: Which IR executes existing SSIS packages in the cloud?

scenarios.title: The late file
scenarios.situation: A daily pipeline runs at 6 AM but the source file sometimes arrives at 7 AM, processing yesterday's file again.
scenarios.prompt: What trigger reacts to the file's arrival?
choices: An event-based trigger on BlobCreated — runs when the file lands, not on a clock
scenarios.why: Event triggers fire on storage events (BlobCreated/Deleted) so pipelines run on data arrival, not on a possibly-wrong schedule. Schedule triggers assume timeliness; event triggers react to reality.
scenarios.hint: What fires the pipeline when the file actually arrives?

scenarios.title: The no-code transform
scenarios.situation: Analysts need to join, aggregate, and clean data visually without writing Spark code.
choices: Mapping data flows — visual transformations executed on Spark clusters
Copy activity — moves data without transforming
scenarios.why: Mapping data flows give a visual designer for joins, aggregations, window functions, and schema handling, executed on ADF-managed Spark — ETL for teams that think in diagrams, with code (wraggle/data flow script) underneath.
scenarios.hint: Visual transformations on Spark without writing Spark — which feature?

scenarios.title: The ten environments
scenarios.situation: Pipelines must run in dev, test, and prod with different servers and containers, but the team maintains three copies of each pipeline.
choices: Parameterization — pipeline/linked-service parameters fed per environment (ARM template parameters or global parameters)
scenarios.why: Parameters let one pipeline definition run anywhere: linked services and datasets take parameters resolved at runtime or deploy time. One definition, N environments — the DRY principle for data engineering.
scenarios.hint: How does one pipeline run against dev, test, and prod?

scenarios.title: The predictable warehouse
scenarios.situation: A retailer runs heavy, predictable nightly ETL plus daytime BI on 20 TB — needs reserved, consistent performance.
choices: Dedicated SQL pool — provisioned DWUs for predictable, heavy workloads
Serverless SQL pool — pay-per-query, for ad-hoc exploration
Spark pool — for the SQL ETL
scenarios.why: Dedicated SQL pools provision compute (DWUs) for consistent, heavy relational workloads — the classic data warehouse. Serverless is pay-per-TB-scanned for ad-hoc queries over the lake; neither replaces the other.
scenarios.hint: Predictable heavy SQL with provisioned performance — which pool?

scenarios.title: The ad-hoc analyst
scenarios.situation: An analyst occasionally queries Parquet files in the lake with T-SQL — a few queries a week, no ETL.
choices: Serverless SQL pool — pay per TB scanned, no infrastructure to manage
scenarios.why: Serverless SQL pools charge per data scanned with zero provisioning — ideal for sporadic analyst queries over lake files. Running dedicated capacity for a few queries a week is pure waste.
scenarios.hint: Occasional T-SQL over lake files — which pool charges only per query?

scenarios.title: The skewed join
scenarios.situation: A Spark job joining a 2 TB fact table to a 50 MB dimension table shuffles for hours.
choices: Broadcast the small dimension table — send it to all executors, avoiding the shuffle
scenarios.why: Broadcast joins replicate the small table to every executor so the big table isn't shuffled — the standard fix for fact-to-small-dimension joins. Shuffling 2 TB to co-locate keys is the cost being avoided.
scenarios.hint: Small dimension, huge fact — how do you avoid shuffling the huge side?

scenarios.title: The bad load
scenarios.situation: A bad ETL load corrupts the Delta table. The team needs yesterday's correct data back.
scenarios.prompt: What Delta Lake feature recovers it?
choices: Time travel — query/restore the table as of a previous version/timestamp
A database backup from last month
scenarios.why: Delta Lake versions every transaction; time travel (VERSION AS OF / TIMESTAMP AS OF) queries or restores prior versions — the built-in undo for bad loads. It's ACID transactions plus history, not just files.
scenarios.hint: What lets you query the table as it looked yesterday?

scenarios.title: The shared exploration
scenarios.situation: Data scientists share analysis as email attachments of scripts; nobody can reproduce anyone's results.
choices: Notebooks with version control (Repos) — shared, reproducible, reviewable analysis
scenarios.why: Databricks Repos bring notebooks under Git version control — shared, diffable, reproducible. Combined with cluster-scoped libraries and jobs, exploration becomes engineering instead of folklore.
scenarios.hint: How do notebooks become reproducible and reviewable?

scenarios.title: The arriving files
scenarios.situation: Thousands of files land in the lake daily; a Structured Streaming job must pick up new ones incrementally without listing the whole directory.
choices: Auto Loader — incrementally processes new files as they arrive, tracking state
A batch job listing everything hourly
scenarios.why: Auto Loader (cloudFiles) uses event notifications or directory listing checkpoints to incrementally ingest new files — efficient, exactly-once-ish, schema-evolution-aware. Full directory scans don't scale with file counts.
scenarios.hint: How do you incrementally ingest thousands of new files a day?

scenarios.title: The ordered device stream
scenarios.situation: A million IoT devices send telemetry; each device's readings must be processed in order, scaled across consumers.
scenarios.prompt: How do Event Hubs partitions serve this?
choices: Partition by device ID — ordering guaranteed within a partition; consumer groups scale processing across partitions
scenarios.why: Event Hubs partitions are the unit of ordering and parallelism: same key → same partition → order preserved; more partitions → more parallel consumers. Partition key design is the core streaming decision.
scenarios.hint: What gives per-device ordering plus parallel consumption?

scenarios.title: The two readers
scenarios.situation: A real-time dashboard and a long-term archive both need every event from the same hub, at their own pace.
choices: Consumer groups — each gets its own offset/cursor over the partitions
Two event hubs with duplicated data
scenarios.why: Consumer groups give each downstream app an independent view (own offsets) of the same partitions — the dashboard reads real-time while the archive lags, neither blocking the other. Duplicating the hub doubles cost for no reason.
scenarios.hint: How do two apps read the same stream at different speeds?

scenarios.title: The 5-minute average
scenarios.situation: A Stream Analytics job must compute each sensor's average temperature over hopping 5-minute windows.
evidence: SELECT sensorId, AVG(temp) FROM input TIMESTAMP BY eventTime GROUP BY sensorId, HoppingWindow(minute, 5, 1)
choices: A hopping (or tumbling) window of 5 minutes with GROUP BY sensor — windows define the aggregation scope
No window — stream jobs aggregate forever
scenarios.why: Stream Analytics windows (tumbling: non-overlapping; hopping: overlapping; sliding; session) bound aggregations in event time. The window choice defines exactly which events each average covers — the heart of stream SQL.
scenarios.hint: What bounds a 'last 5 minutes' aggregation in a stream?

scenarios.title: The delayed sensor
scenarios.situation: Sensors buffer readings offline and send them hours late; the stream job currently drops them silently.
choices: Late-arrival tolerance and out-of-order policies — configure how late events are admitted vs. dropped
scenarios.why: Stream systems define lateness policies: how far behind event time you'll still accept data. Real devices go offline — the design must choose between dropping late data or accommodating it, explicitly.
scenarios.hint: Events arrive hours late. What policy decides their fate?

scenarios.title: The replay need
scenarios.situation: Compliance requires every raw event retained for 2 years and replayable into new analytics.
scenarios.prompt: What Event Hubs feature provides this?
choices: Capture — automatically writes raw events to ADLS/Blob in Avro/Parquet for replay and batch analysis
Consumer groups — don't retain raw files
scenarios.why: Event Hubs Capture lands the raw stream to storage (Avro/Parquet) continuously — the immutable raw record for compliance, replay, and batch reprocessing. Retention keeps events in the hub briefly; Capture archives them durably.
scenarios.hint: What archives the raw stream to the lake automatically?

scenarios.title: The downstream outage
scenarios.situation: The stream job's database sink goes down for an hour; events must not be lost and the job must catch up after.
scenarios.prompt: What property of the design saves the data?
choices: Durable buffered ingestion (Event Hubs retention) + checkpointing — the job resumes from the last checkpoint and replays
scenarios.why: Event Hubs retains events for the configured period; streaming jobs checkpoint offsets, so after a sink outage they resume and catch up from the buffer. Durability lives in the log (the hub), not in the processor's memory.
scenarios.hint: Where does the data wait safely during a sink outage?

scenarios.title: The pipeline credential
scenarios.situation: ADF pipelines connect to SQL and Storage with stored passwords that expire and break nightly loads.
choices: Managed identity for Data Factory — grant it data-plane roles on each source/sink; no stored passwords
scenarios.why: ADF's system-assigned managed identity authenticates to Azure data stores via RBAC — no credentials to rotate, expire, or leak. Stored credentials in linked services are the fragile pattern this replaces.
scenarios.hint: How do pipelines authenticate with zero stored secrets?

scenarios.title: The public lake
scenarios.situation: The data lake's storage account allows public network access; auditors flag PII-adjacent datasets.
choices: Private endpoints for the lake + storage firewall denying public access, with ADF/Synapse connecting privately
scenarios.why: Data-plane privacy needs private endpoints (lake traffic stays in the VNet) plus public-access disabled at the account level. ADF needs a managed VNet/IR or private endpoints to reach it — network design is part of data security.
scenarios.hint: How do you make lake traffic never touch the public internet?

scenarios.title: The key control
scenarios.situation: A customer contract requires the company — not Microsoft — to control the encryption keys for their data lake.
choices: Customer-managed keys (CMK) in Key Vault — Microsoft still encrypts, but key lifecycle is yours
scenarios.why: CMK moves key control (creation, rotation, revocation) to your Key Vault while the service still performs encryption. Revoking the key renders the data unreadable — the contractual 'we control the keys' proof.
scenarios.hint: Who controls key lifecycle with CMK, and what does revocation do?

scenarios.title: The regional analysts
scenarios.situation: Analysts in each region must see only their region's rows in a shared sales table.
scenarios.prompt: What enforces this in the warehouse?
choices: Row-level security — filter predicates by user/region so one table serves all with scoped visibility
scenarios.why: RLS applies security predicates (e.g., WHERE region = USER's region) transparently — one table, per-user visibility. It's the standard multi-tenant analytics pattern, enforced by the engine, not by convention.
scenarios.hint: One table, each user sees only their rows — which feature?

scenarios.title: The unknown PII
scenarios.situation: Nobody knows which lake datasets contain customer emails; a privacy request is due in 72 hours.
choices: Microsoft Purview scans with classification rules — auto-labels PII across the lake with a searchable catalog
scenarios.why: Purview's scanners classify sensitive data (emails, SSNs, etc.) across ADLS, SQL, and more, building a searchable data map — the only feasible answer at lake scale under a deadline.
scenarios.hint: What scans the whole lake and labels sensitive data automatically?

scenarios.title: The suspicious query
scenarios.situation: A DBA needs a tamper-evident record of who queried the finance database and when.
choices: SQL auditing — logs database events to Log Analytics/Storage for forensic review
scenarios.why: Azure SQL Auditing records database events (logins, queries, permission changes) to immutable storage — the compliance trail for 'who touched the data'. Application logs see app behavior, not direct database access.
scenarios.hint: Which feature logs database access for forensics?

scenarios.title: The failed pipeline
scenarios.situation: A 3 AM pipeline fails silently; the team learns about it from angry analysts at 9 AM.
choices: ADF alerts on pipeline run failures + Log Analytics diagnostics — alert rules notify on failure, not on user complaints
scenarios.why: ADF emits run metrics and diagnostic logs; alert rules on failed pipeline/activity runs (via action groups) notify immediately. Silent failures are a monitoring gap, not a pipeline bug.
scenarios.hint: What notifies the team the moment a pipeline run fails?

scenarios.title: The slow dedicated pool
scenarios.situation: Queries on the dedicated SQL pool suddenly slow down; the team suspects concurrency or skew.
choices: Synapse Studio Monitor hub — query history, durations, resource utilization, and data-skew insights
scenarios.why: The Monitor hub surfaces executed queries with durations, queued time, DWU usage, and distribution skew — the evidence for 'concurrency vs. skew vs. bad query'. Monitoring starts with the workload's own telemetry.
scenarios.hint: Which hub shows query history and resource use for Synapse?

scenarios.title: The failed job run
scenarios.situation: A Databricks job fails intermittently; the error is in the driver log nobody looks at.
choices: Cluster log delivery to ADLS + job run alerts — logs persist beyond cluster termination for post-mortems
scenarios.why: Clusters are ephemeral; without log delivery, driver/executor logs vanish on termination. Delivering logs to storage plus alerting on job failure turns intermittent failures into investigable incidents.
scenarios.hint: Clusters die; how do their logs survive for investigation?

scenarios.title: The broken column
scenarios.situation: A dashboard column shows wrong values; nobody knows which pipeline or transformation feeds it.
choices: Data lineage — Purview or ADF lineage views trace column-level flow from source to report
scenarios.why: Lineage maps data flow across pipelines, notebooks, and datasets — impact analysis ('what breaks if I change this?') and root-cause ('where did this value come from?') in one view. Undocumented pipelines make this impossible.
scenarios.hint: What shows a column's path from source to dashboard?

scenarios.title: The schema change
scenarios.situation: A source system adds a column; the pipeline breaks instead of adapting.
choices: Schema drift tolerance (ADF data flows) / Delta Lake schema evolution — allow and map new columns explicitly
Deleting the new column at the source
scenarios.why: Production pipelines must expect schema change: ADF data flows support schema drift; Delta Lake supports schema evolution/merging. The design decision is whether new columns flow through, get mapped, or get quarantined — explicitly.
scenarios.hint: Sources change schemas. What keeps pipelines from breaking?

scenarios.title: The runaway spark
scenarios.situation: A Databricks workspace bill triples; someone left a large interactive cluster running all month.
choices: Cluster policies + auto-termination + budgets/alerts — guardrails on size, idle timeout, and spend
scenarios.why: Cluster policies constrain allowed sizes and auto-terminate idle clusters; budgets alert on spend. Compute left running is the #1 data-platform cost leak — prevention beats forensics.
scenarios.hint: What stops an idle cluster from billing all month?

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time a data pipeline you owned failed in production.
points: The failure and its downstream impact

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to design for data quality issues you couldn't control.
Tell me about a time you optimized a slow data process.
Describe a disagreement about data modeling or architecture.
Tell me about a time you handled sensitive data under compliance constraints.
Describe a time you automated away manual data work.
Tell me about a time you had to explain a data issue to non-technical stakeholders.
Why are you pursuing the Azure Data Engineer certification, and what data platforms do you want to own?

chat.persona: You are a rigorous data-engineering interviewer running a mock DP-203 assessment. Demand physical-design reasoning: partitioning, file formats, streaming semantics, and failure behavior. Ask 'what happens at 10x scale' and 'what breaks when the source changes'.
